### Summary When an application appends to an existing PDF with `Image.save(..., format="PDF", append=True)`, Pillow parses that file with `PdfParser`. Two recursive parsers have no effective bound. `linearize_page_tree` follows `/Kids` with no visited set or depth limit, so a cyclic or duplicated page tree recurses without end. `read_prev_trailer` rejects only an exactly repeated `/Prev` offset, so a long chain of unique offsets still recurses. The trailer-loop guard added for CVE-2026-42310 does not cover either case.  ### Details `linearize_page_tree` recurses on `/Kids` with no cycle or depth check:  - `src/PIL/PdfParser.py:1078-1092`  `read_prev_trailer` catches only a repeated offset:  - `src/PIL/PdfParser.py:697-720` (the `processed_offsets` check at `:714-718` is the CVE-2026-42310 fix; a unique-offset chain slips past it)  ### PoC ```python from PIL import PdfParser  # A page tree whose /Pages nodes reference each other in a cycle (2 -> 3 -> 2). objs = {     1: b"<< /Type /Catalog /Pages 2 0 R >>",     2: b"<< /Type /Pages /Kids [3 0 R] /Count 1 >>",     3: b"<< /Type /Pages /Kids [2 0 R] /Count 1 >>", } buf = bytearray(b"%PDF-1.4
") off = {} for oid in (1, 2, 3):     off[oid] = len(buf)     buf += b"%d 0 obj
" % oid + objs[oid] + b"
endobj
" xref = len(buf) buf += b"xref
0 4
0000000000 65535 f 
" buf += b"".join(b"%010d 00000 n 
" % off[o] for o in (1, 2, 3)) buf += b"trailer
<< /Root 1 0 R /Size 4 >>
startxref
%d
%%%%EOF
" % xref open("poc.pdf", "wb").write(buf)  PdfParser.PdfParser("poc.pdf", mode="r+b")   # append=True parses the existing file the same way ```  Run it: ``` $ python 11_poc.py RecursionError: maximum recursion depth exceeded ```  The 315-byte file triggers the recursion on parse. A duplicated (non-cyclic) `/Kids` tree instead produces super-linear CPU and memory work, and a long unique-offset `/Prev` chain triggers the trailer-side recursion.  ### Impact A service that appends to user-supplied PDFs, for example a stamping or watermarking pipeline, can be driven into uncaught recursion or heavy CPU and memory use before any image is written. Follow-up to CVE-2026-42310. Since Pillow's policy discourages filing plain Python exceptions as denial of service, lead with the cyclic-tree case, which burns CPU and memory rather than only raising `RecursionError`. The fix is a visited set plus a depth limit in both parsers.

``` ============================================================================ GIF seek keeps rejected size after DecompressionBombError, allowing DoS Location: src/PIL/GifImagePlugin.py:293 in GifImageFile._seek() Commit: a707c6b21c313880d0771e54965d142dd42358b6 ============================================================================ ``` A GIF of about 60 bytes can make Pillow allocate gigabytes of memory. This affects applications that catch the "image too large" error raised while stepping to a later animation frame and then keep using the same image object. Pillow correctly refuses the oversized frame, but it stores the refused dimensions on the image object anyway, and later operations size their memory from them. An attacker who can upload a GIF to such a service can exhaust its memory: the process either fails with an out-of-memory error after committing gigabytes, or is killed by the operating system. There is no memory corruption. The bug is in `GifImageFile._seek()` (`src/PIL/GifImagePlugin.py:292-294`). When a frame's extent enlarges the image, the code assigns the new size to `self._size` and only then calls `Image._decompression_bomb_check()`. Nothing restores the old size when `DecompressionBombError` is raised, because `seek()` only rolls back on `EOFError`. After the caught error, `im.size` reports the rejected size while the pixel buffer `im.im` is still the 1×1 first frame. Because the extent is a 16-bit offset plus a 16-bit size, that rejected size can be as large as 131070×131070. In the attached reproducer, the rejected size is 40000×40000. A retried `seek(1)` followed by `load()` then reaches `load_prepare()`, which calls `Image.core.fill()` with that size to decode a single pixel. Peak memory rises from 17 MiB to 1700 MiB before a 3 GiB address-space cap stops the next allocation. `Image.new("RGB", im.size, ...)` and `rotate(..., expand=True)` also allocate from the stale size. The default paths are unaffected: plain `Image.open()` plus `load()`, `ImageSequence.Iterator`, and `n_frames`/`is_animated`. The ordering was introduced in c9f1b35e9810 ("Added GIF decompression bomb check", 2022-06-30, first released in 9.2.0), the check added for CVE-2022-45198. The two dispose-extent checks later in the same function already validate before using the size, and the attached patch makes this check follow the same order. ## Details `GifImageFile._seek()` lets a later frame enlarge the image, and performs the decompression-bomb check for the new size only *after* storing it on the object: ```python # src/PIL/GifImagePlugin.py:289-294 (GifImageFile._seek) x0, y0 = i16(s, 0), i16(s, 2) x1, y1 = x0 + i16(s, 4), y0 + i16(s, 6) if (x1 > self.size[0] or y1 > self.size[1]) and update_image: self._size = max(x1, self.size[0]), max(y1, self.size[1]) # state mutated Image._decompression_bomb_check(self._size) # ...then validated ``` `_decompression_bomb_check()` (`src/PIL/Image.py:3586`) raises `DecompressionBombError` for anything above `2 * MAX_IMAGE_PIXELS` (178 956 970 px by default), but by then `self._size` already holds the rejected value and nothing restores it: `seek()` (`GifImagePlugin.py:166-179`) only rolls back on `EOFError`, and `_seek(0)` only ever grows `_size`. The object that the application still holds therefore reports `im.size == (40000, 40000)` while `im.im` is the 1×1 buffer of frame 0. Compare the two dispose-extent checks a few lines further down in the same function (`GifImagePlugin.py:383` and `:407`), which call `_decompression_bomb_check(dispose_size)` *before* the corresponding `Image.core.fill()`, and `TiffImagePlugin.load_prepare()` (`src/PIL/TiffImagePlugin.py:1319-1321`), which checks `_tile_size` before allocating from it. With this 60-byte GIF (hex) ``` 47494638396101000100800000000000ffffff GIF89a, 1x1 screen, 2-entry global palette 2c000000000100010000 02 024401 00 frame 0: 1x1 @ (0,0), LZW data 2c00000000409c409c00 frame 1 descriptor: 40000x40000 @ (0,0) 2c000000000100010000 02 024401 00 another 1x1 frame 3b trailer ``` `Image.open()` succeeds (`im.size == (1, 1)`), `im.seek(1)` raises `DecompressionBombError: Image size (1600000000 pixels) exceeds limit of 178956970 pixels`, and afterwards `im.size == (40000, 40000)`, `im.im.size == (1, 1)`, `im.tell() == 0`. What happens next depends on what the application does with the object, but several ordinary operations take their dimensions from `im.size` rather than from the C buffer: - Retrying `im.seek(1)`. The failed `_seek` left `self.__offset == 0` and the file pointer just past the 9-byte descriptor, so the retry parses whatever follows — in the file above, a valid 1×1 frame — and succeeds. `im.load()` then runs `GifImageFile.load_prepare()`: ```python # src/PIL/GifImagePlugin.py:452-456 elif self.mode in ("RGB", "RGBA"): self._prev_im = self.im if self._frame_palette: self.im = Image.core.fill("P", self.size, self._frame_transparency or 0) ``` which allocates and `memset`s a 40000×40000 "P" image (1.6 GB) to decode a 1×1 tile into, and `load_end()` (`GifImagePlugin.py:485-491`) fills a second one and converts it to RGB (another 1.6 GB + 6.4 GB). - `im.rotate(angle, expand=True)` for a non-multiple-of-90 angle, or the common flatten-onto-background idiom `Image.new("RGB", im.size, bg)`, allocate from `im.size` as well (measured on an object poisoned to 20000×20000: `rotate(45, expand=True)` completes and touches 776 MiB; `Image.new("RGB", im.size, "white")` touches 1.5 GiB). Operations that pass `im.size` as a box against the real buffer (`thumbnail`, `resize`, `save`) fail with `ValueError`/`SystemError` instead. The extent fields are 16-bit offset plus 16-bit size, so the stored size can be pushed to 131070×131070 (17.2 Gpx; 17 GB for mode "P", 69 GB for "RGB"/"RGBA" storage), 96× the error threshold. `n_frames` / `is_animated` are not affected: they call `_seek(frame, update_image=False)`, which skips the `_size` assignment (the file above reports `n_frames == 2`, `is_animated == True` and leaves `im.size` at 1×1). ## Impact A remote user who can upload a GIF to a service that (a) seeks animation frames and (b) catches the exception from `seek()` — a broad `except Exception` around a `while True: im.seek(im.tell()+1)` frame-collection loop, or an explicit `except DecompressionBombError: log and continue` — and then keeps using the same `Image` object, ends up driving allocations of 1.6 GB to tens of GB from a 60-byte file: `MemoryError` after the process has committed gigabytes, or an OOM kill of the worker when no address-space limit is set. The `MAX_IMAGE_PIXELS` guard fires, but does not actually keep the rejected dimensions out of the object it is guarding. The precondition is real application behaviour but not the default path: `Image.open(); im.load()` is unaffected, and `ImageSequence.Iterator` propagates the error out of the `for` statement (a `try` inside the loop body does not swallow it). Hence low severity. This is adjacent to the GIF extent bomb check added for CVE-2022-45198: the ordering was introduced with that check in `c9f1b35e9810` ("Added GIF decompression bomb check", 2022-06-30), first released in Pillow 9.2.0. Before it, the same size growth happened with no check at all; the check introduced there is the one that runs too late. ## Reproducing `repro` is a single Python script run against the installed Pillow. It needs about 1.7 GB of free RAM. 1. **`setup_env()`** caps the process address space at 3 GiB with `RLIMIT_AS`, so the oversized allocations end in `MemoryError` instead of the OOM killer. It then opens the 60-byte GIF shown above, built in memory by `bomb_gif()`. The GIF contains a 1×1 screen and a 1×1 frame 0, so `Image.open()` passes its own bomb check. Next comes a bare frame-1 image descriptor that declares 40000×40000 (1.6 Gpx, about 9× the error threshold). A real 1×1 frame follows it. 2. **`poc()`** calls `im.seek(1)` and catches `DecompressionBombError`, the way an application that skips bad frames would. 3. **First check: the state is inconsistent.** The script prints `im.size` next to the real pixel buffer `im.im.size`. If the rejected frame had left the object unchanged, both would be `(1, 1)`. On the affected code `im.size` is `(40000, 40000)`. 4. **Second check: memory use.** The script retries `im.seek(1)`, which now parses the trailing 1×1 frame, and calls `im.load()`. It prints the process's peak RSS before and after. `load_prepare()` sizes its `Image.core.fill()` from `im.size`, so loading a single pixel fills a 1.6 GB buffer before the 3 GiB cap stops the next allocation. Expected output on the affected tree: ``` open(): 60-byte GIF, size=(1, 1) seek(1) raised as intended: Image size (1600000000 pixels) exceeds limit of 178956970 pixels, could be decompression bomb DOS attack. after the caught error: im.size=(40000, 40000), pixel buffer im.im.size=(1, 1) seek(1) + load() of a 1x1 frame: MemoryError at the 3 GiB cap; peak RSS 18 MiB -> 1700 MiB BUG ``` The script prints `BUG` only if both checks hold: the over-limit size stayed on the object after the exception, and peak RSS grew by more than 1000 MiB while loading a 1×1 frame. Otherwise it prints `OK`. With the attached patch applied, it prints `im.size=(1, 1)`, peak RSS stays at about 23 MiB, and the last line is `OK`. ## Suggested fix The attached patch validates before mutating in `GifImageFile._seek()` (`src/PIL/GifImagePlugin.py:292-294`): the enlarged extent is computed into a local, passed to `_decompression_bomb_check()`, and only then assigned to `self._size`, matching the order of the two `dispose_size` checks further down the same function. A rejected frame therefore leaves the object in its pre-seek state; valid files behave as before, and the exception is still raised at the same point: ```diff --- a/src/PIL/GifImagePlugin.py +++ b/src/PIL/GifImagePlugin.py @@ -290,8 +290,9 @@ class GifImageFile(ImageFile.ImageFile): x0, y0 = i16(s, 0), i16(s, 2) x1, y1 = x0 + i16(s, 4), y0 + i16(s, 6) if (x1 > self.size[0] or y1 > self.size[1]) and update_image: - self._size = max(x1, self.size[0]), max(y1, self.size[1]) - Image._decompression_bomb_check(self._size) + size = max(x1, self.size[0]), max(y1, self.size[1]) + Image._decompression_bomb_check(size) + self._size = size frame_dispose_extent = x0, y0, x1, y1 flags = s[8] ``` `n_frames` / `is_animated` go through `update_image=False` and are unaffected. The patch also extends `test_exception_gif_extents` in `Tests/test_decompression_bomb.py` to assert that `im.size` is unchanged after the `DecompressionBombError`. It does not change `seek()` itself; optionally, `seek()` could also treat `DecompressionBombError` like `EOFError` and re-seek to `last_frame`, so that a retried `seek()` does not resume parsing from the middle of the rejected frame. ## The patch GIF: run the decompression bomb check on an enlarging frame's extent before storing it in self._size Applies to `src/PIL/GifImagePlugin.py` at the commit above. ```diff diff --git a/Tests/test_decompression_bomb.py b/Tests/test_decompression_bomb.py index 98d833736..83cc785fc 100644 --- a/Tests/test_decompression_bomb.py +++ b/Tests/test_decompression_bomb.py @@ -63,6 +63,9 @@ class TestDecompressionBomb: with pytest.raises(Image.DecompressionBombError): im.seek(1) + # The rejected frame should not have changed the image size + assert im.size == (100, 100) + def test_exception_gif_zero_width(self, monkeypatch: pytest.MonkeyPatch) -> None: # Set limit to trigger exception on the test file monkeypatch.setattr(Image, "MAX_IMAGE_PIXELS", 4 * 64 * 128) diff --git a/src/PIL/GifImagePlugin.py b/src/PIL/GifImagePlugin.py index 11fb180fc..f9bda06c2 100644 --- a/src/PIL/GifImagePlugin.py +++ b/src/PIL/GifImagePlugin.py @@ -290,8 +290,9 @@ class GifImageFile(ImageFile.ImageFile): x0, y0 = i16(s, 0), i16(s, 2) x1, y1 = x0 + i16(s, 4), y0 + i16(s, 6) if (x1 > self.size[0] or y1 > self.size[1]) and update_image: - self._size = max(x1, self.size[0]), max(y1, self.size[1]) - Image._decompression_bomb_check(self._size) + size = max(x1, self.size[0]), max(y1, self.size[1]) + Image._decompression_bomb_check(size) + self._size = size frame_dispose_extent = x0, y0, x1, y1 flags = s[8] ``` ## The reproducer
Reproducer — repro, 2,474 bytes (click to open) Its last line is `BUG` when the issue triggers and `OK` when it does not. Re-run on a clean build of that commit it printed `BUG`. ```python #!/usr/bin/env python3 # GifImageFile._seek() stores a frame's enlarged size in self._size and only # *then* runs the decompression-bomb check. The check raises, but the object # keeps the rejected 40000x40000 size over its real 1x1 pixel buffer, and the # next load() allocates from that size: 1.6+ GB for a 60-byte GIF. import io import resource import struct from PIL import Image BOMB = 40000 # 40000x40000 = 1.6 Gpx, ~9x the DecompressionBombError threshold LIMIT = 2 * Image.MAX_IMAGE_PIXELS def frame_1x1(): # image descriptor at (0,0) 1x1, then a 1-pixel LZW stream return b"," + struct.pack(" LIMIT and im.im.size == (1, 1) # Effect: retrying the seek lands on the real 1x1 frame, but load() sizes its # buffers from the poisoned im.size. before = peak_rss_mib() im.seek(1) try: im.load() outcome = "completed" except MemoryError: outcome = "MemoryError at the 3 GiB cap" after = peak_rss_mib() print(f"seek(1) + load() of a 1x1 frame: {outcome}; peak RSS {before} MiB -> {after} MiB") ballooned = after - before > 1000 print("BUG" if poisoned and ballooned else "OK") ```

### Summary A PPM or PGM file can declare a width of 0, which Pillow accepts, producing an image of size `(0, N)`. Passing that image to `ImageMorph.MorphOp.apply()` makes the native morphology code index a row buffer at `outrow[width - 1]`, which is `outrow[-1]` when the width is 0. The process crashes.  ### Details The PPM parser reads width and height with no lower-bound check:  - `src/PIL/PpmImagePlugin.py:119`  The native `apply()` writes the row edges with no guard that the width is positive:  - `src/_imagingmorph.c:81` sets `outrow[0] = outrow[width - 1] = 0;`  `match()` and `get_on_pixels()` use the same edge-indexing pattern.  ### PoC ```python from PIL import Image, ImageMorph  # A width-0 image (also producible from a crafted PPM header). apply() indexes # outrow[width - 1] == outrow[-1] in native code. im = Image.new("L", (0, 5)) ImageMorph.MorphOp(op_name="dilation4").apply(im) ```  Run it: ``` $ python 03_poc.py Segmentation fault (core dumped) ```  Observed on a source build of commit `3e2ab96`.  Under AddressSanitizer: ``` ==ERROR: AddressSanitizer: SEGV on unknown address (pc ... in apply)     #0 apply   src/_imagingmorph.c:81 SUMMARY: AddressSanitizer: SEGV src/_imagingmorph.c:81 in apply ``` With width 0 the `outrow[width - 1]` write lands on an unmapped page, so it surfaces as a SEGV pinned to the edge-write line rather than a redzone overflow.  ### Impact Out-of-bounds write in a C extension. Affects any application that runs a morphology operation on an image opened from untrusted input. Result is a crash and possible memory corruption.

## Summary  A small attacker-supplied TIFF can be opened and loaded normally, then reach an out-of-bounds read when an application saves it back to TIFF with retained metadata. The fixed reproducer is a 1×1, 16-bit grayscale, PackBits-compressed TIFF containing tag 320 (ColorMap) with **768 SHORT values**: three zero-filled planes of 256 entries each. No Python object is forged and no metadata is injected after loading.  Pillow's TIFF encoder allocates **768 × 2 = 1536 bytes**, then passes three plane pointers separated by 256 SHORT entries to libtiff. With `BitsPerSample = 16`, libtiff instead expects **65536 SHORT values per plane** and attempts a **131072-byte read** from a plane pointer. Existing ASAN observations identify a heap-buffer-overflow READ crossing the 1536-byte allocation made in `PyImaging_LibTiffEncoderNew`.  The malformed ColorMap need not be a valid palette for this grayscale image. The issue is that accepted metadata is forwarded on save without reconciling the fixed plane extent with the effective sample depth. Opening/loading alone is not the demonstrated fault; the encoder path is required.  ## Impact and prerequisites  An application must accept the input, retain the relevant TIFF metadata, and invoke the libtiff-backed TIFF save path. The observed consequence is an out-of-bounds read and ASAN termination. Process-memory exposure during encoding is a potential consequence, **not demonstrated by extracting arbitrary heap contents in this report**. No arbitrary read primitive, full memory-disclosure chain, code execution, address-space bypass, or cross-process effect is claimed.  The 131072-byte attempted copy is not the number of bytes proven disclosed. This report does not run a synthetic-canary serializer or collect an unsanitized encoded output.  ## Tested environment and limits of the evidence  The existing observations were recorded on August 30, 2026, with **CPython 3.11.8 on macOS ARM64**, using the unmodified official **Pillow 12.3.0** wheel and its bundled **libtiff 4.7.1**:  - Wheel: `pillow-12.3.0-cp311-cp311-macosx_11_0_arm64.whl` - Wheel size: `4785266` bytes - Wheel SHA-256: `37d6d0a00072fd2948eb22bce7e1475f34569d90c87c59f7a2ec59541b77f7a6` - Pillow source revision: `bb1d8e8ab8d29048624d96e3ee53cecf7c13d13d` - Bundled libtiff SHA-256: `e8988717b7470394a47d5ccd343130796b24ee70b6d885d3818e0e0b53238be1`  Apple's ASAN runtime was injected at process startup. This is **not an ASAN-rebuilt Pillow wheel**; allocation/memcpy interception detects the reported boundary violation, but the wheel's native instructions are not comprehensively instrumented.  Only this concrete full-package environment is established here. No affected-version range, current development-branch result, or patched release is asserted. Severity is **Unknown**; no CVSS score is proposed.  Separate earlier evidence reached the original Pillow 8.0.1 encoder constructor compiled as a component against a modern Python/libtiff environment. **That was not a complete Pillow 8.0.1 installation** and does not establish the historical package's full runtime behavior. It is not part of this reproducer or an affected-version range.  ## Observed evidence and controls  The earlier integration harness performed the natural sequence `Image.open(BytesIO(input))`, `image.load()`, then `image.save(BytesIO(), format="TIFF")`, without replacing the image's metadata. Each case was recorded three times:  | Original fixture | Bytes | Recorded result | | --- | ---: | --- | | `colormap16` | 1685 | Loaded as `I;16`; save terminated with ASAN exit 86, READ of size 131072 crossing a 1536-byte heap region (3/3). | | `colormap8` | 1684 | Same fixed ColorMap, but 8-bit samples; save succeeded and retained SHORT/count 768 (3/3). | | `colormap_absent` | 137 | Same 16-bit geometry without ColorMap; save succeeded (3/3). |  Address-free summary of the recorded native diagnostic:  ```text AddressSanitizer: heap-buffer-overflow READ of size 131072 0 bytes after 1536-byte region Copy path: memcpy -> _TIFFmemcpy -> setByteArray -> _TIFFsetShortArrayExt            -> _TIFFVSetField -> TIFFVSetField -> ImagingLibTiffSetField            -> PyImaging_LibTiffEncoderNew Allocation: calloc -> PyImaging_LibTiffEncoderNew ```  Input SHA-256 values (also enforced inside the script):  - `colormap16`: `5f38e0ead90b97949fb0c98c63f9c68d00ba9181db6631ecb8927376dcc75f4d` - `colormap8`: `fdb26d9135549ed44824901985086c5ee4f06515699ca3291e498c523935405c` - `colormap_absent`: `bd54979624f3ffb713342e0458caff9e17c477f940cda2f0960feebfabbc9556`  ## Root cause and source references  - [Pillow `src/encode.c`, lines 870–899, pinned revision](https://github.com/python-pillow/Pillow/blob/bb1d8e8ab8d29048624d96e3ee53cecf7c13d13d/src/encode.c#L870): the ColorMap tuple must contain exactly 768 entries; a 1536-byte allocation is passed with a fixed stride of 256. The check does not reconcile that extent with `BitsPerSample`. - [Pillow `src/PIL/TiffImagePlugin.py`, lines 1944–1991, pinned revision](https://github.com/python-pillow/Pillow/blob/bb1d8e8ab8d29048624d96e3ee53cecf7c13d13d/src/PIL/TiffImagePlugin.py#L1944): save carries supplied tags into the libtiff encoder and sorts the tags, so sample depth is established before ColorMap. - [libtiff `tif_dir.c`, lines 441–448, pinned revision](https://gitlab.com/libtiff/libtiff/-/blob/5fe20d0e9aba49a6a350ed533459d1505203838f/libtiff/tif_dir.c#L441): `TIFFTAG_COLORMAP` computes the per-plane count as `1L << td->td_bitspersample` and copies that many SHORTs from each pointer.  The reported boundary is Pillow's construction of a fixed-sized array for a native API whose required size depends on metadata; this does not establish a standalone libtiff defect for a correctly sized caller buffer.  ## Prior art and disclosure scope  [Pillow PR #5148](https://github.com/python-pillow/Pillow/pull/5148), merged December 28, 2020, is related TIFF metadata prior art, but its archived diff replaces a short-lived stack field-name pointer with the persistent literal `"CustomField"`. That is a **different field-name-lifetime fix**, not this plane-size mismatch. The reviewed material does not establish an exact prior public report or fix for this root, and **novelty is not asserted**. This specific report remains NOT_SENT; association with other observations is not a prior disclosure of it.  ## Reproduction instructions  Use an **already reviewed, existing** installation of the exact wheel above, an existing compatible macOS ARM64 CPython 3.11 interpreter, and an existing compatible Apple ASAN runtime. `--package-path` is the absolute directory containing `PIL`, not the `PIL` directory itself. The script does not install, download, build, patch, or submit anything. It checks selected key package files against the original installation's hashes and checks the loaded package/version; these checks are not a full installation attestation.  Save the complete Python block below as `reproduce.py` and run:  ```sh python3.11 -I -S -B reproduce.py \   --package-path /absolute/path/to/reviewed/site-packages \   --asan-runtime /absolute/path/to/reviewed/libclang_rt.asan_osx_dynamic.dylib ```  Both arguments are required. The runtime must be loaded at child startup, not by late `dlopen`. Each child resolves `__asan_init`, `__asan_address_is_poisoned`, and `__asan_region_is_poisoned` in its actual process symbol table **before importing Pillow or opening a fixture**. Merely setting `DYLD_INSERT_LIBRARIES` is not accepted as proof of ASAN availability. A missing symbol or package mismatch prevents the operation.  Each of the three cases runs once in a separate child with a **30-second wall limit, 10-second hard CPU limit, core dumps disabled, and 1 MiB regular-file-size limit**. The parent supplies a clean allowlisted environment, isolated Python startup (`-I -S -B`), an empty temporary working directory, no stdin, and a 128 KiB combined pipe-output cap. Timeout/output-cap handling kills the child's process group. These limits are containment measures, not a security sandbox. No TIFF is written to disk. Temporary directories are removed; raw diagnostics are never forwarded or persisted.  The compressed/base64 constants below are the **unchanged original benign TIFF fixtures**, with decompressed size and SHA-256 checks. There are no external fixture dependencies. The standalone script supplied with this description is byte-for-byte the same as this block.  **Separate August 31, 2026 inline validation:** the exact embedded standalone script passed all three fixed cases: one ASan READ of 131,072 bytes crossing a 1,536-byte allocation and two passing controls. Child guards and limits passed, with no timeout. This is additional bounded evidence, separate from earlier runs; no new build, install, full historical chain or older-version integration replay was performed.  ## Expected results from the standalone script  Cases run in order: `colormap8`, `colormap_absent`, `colormap16`. Every printed line should have `guard_passed: true`, `within_limits: true`, and `expected_observation: true`. The first two require successful saves and the expected retained sample-depth/ColorMap fields. The last requires ASAN exit 86 **and** the specific READ/extent/stack signatures, not merely any crash. Only the two controls inspect encoded metadata; the unsafe case never exports an encoded TIFF.  The parent exits 0 only if all three expectations match; 1 means a case did not match (including guard failure or a changed ASAN diagnostic), and 2 means parent setup failed. Anyone who can get an application to open their image, and can see something produced from its pixels (a thumbnail, a preview, a converted copy), can read heap memory that the process had previously used and freed. This works in the default configuration: opening and loading the 478-byte file succeeds with no error or warning, and every row below the first eight holds stale memory instead of picture content. The bug is in `_decodeStrip()` in `src/libImaging/TiffDecode.c`, and `_decodeTile()` has the same shape. The function `realloc()`s `state->buffer` to `TIFFStripSize()` bytes without initialising it and calls `TIFFReadEncodedStrip()`. Whenever that call does not return -1, it copies all `RowsPerStrip` rows of the buffer into the image. libtiff's JPEG codec only warns when the JPEG embedded in a strip has fewer rows than the strip, and Pillow silences libtiff warnings. The codec decodes the rows that exist and still returns the full strip size, so the untouched remainder is copied out as pixels. libtiff's Group 4 fax codec behaves the same way for a stream that ends early. The attached reproducer builds a 256×256 TIFF whose single strip or tile is a 256×8 JPEG. Before loading it, the script frees buffers filled with `b"LEAK"`. ### Summary  Pillow's libImaging `_decodeTile` decoder, used to decode tiled TIFF images, allocates a per-tile buffer using `realloc(state->buffer, TIFFTileSize(tiff))`. After each `TIFFReadTile` it then iterates `tile_y` from 0 up to `current_tile_length` and calls the configured row unpacker (here `copy4`) with the source pointer `state->buffer + tile_y * row_byte_size`. When libtiff returns a `tile_bytes_size` smaller than the worst-case `row_byte_size * tile_length`, the inner stride-and-copy loop walks past the realloc'd region and `copy4` performs a 1024-byte `memcpy` that reads up to `(tile_length-1) * row_byte_size + row_byte_size` bytes from a buffer sized only to `tile_bytes_size`. The supplied PoC TIFF triggers a 1024-byte over-read exactly 0 bytes past a 196608-byte allocation. An attacker who can convince a Pillow-using application to decode a crafted TIFF can trigger a process crash (DoS) and may cause adjacent heap memory to be copied into the decoded pixel buffer.  ### Details  Pillow's TIFF decoder, when libtiff reports the file is tiled, takes the `_decodeTile` path. The function:  1. Asks libtiff for `TIFFTileSize(tiff)` (the bytes-per-tile) and `TIFFTileRowSize(tiff)` (the bytes per row *as stored by libtiff*). 2. Reallocates `state->buffer` to exactly `tile_bytes_size`. 3. For each tile origin `(x, y)` and each plane, calls `TIFFReadTile` into `state->buffer`, then walks the tile row by row, calling the configured `ImagingShuffler` (here `copy4`) on each row's worth of source bytes.  The validation done before the loop is:  ```c if (tile_bytes_size > ((tile_length * state->bits / planes + 7) / 8) * tile_width) {     state->errcode = IMAGING_CODEC_BROKEN;     return -1; } ```  This rejects oversized libtiff tiles, but it does **not** reject *undersized* ones — i.e. the case where libtiff returns a `tile_bytes_size` strictly **less** than `row_byte_size * tile_length`. The loop body, however, indexes into the buffer assuming the buffer is at least `row_byte_size * tile_length` bytes long.  ### Vulnerable Code  ```c // src/libImaging/TiffDecode.c:446-490 — _decodeTile new_data = realloc(state->buffer, state->bytes);   // bytes = tile_bytes_size if (!new_data) { ... } state->buffer = new_data;  for (y = state->yoff; y < state->ysize; y += tile_length) {     for (plane = 0; plane < planes; plane++) {         ImagingShuffler shuffler = unpackers[plane];         for (x = state->xoff; x < state->xsize; x += tile_width) {             if (TIFFReadTile(tiff, (tdata_t)state->buffer, x, y, 0, plane) == -1) { ... }              current_tile_width  = min((INT32)tile_width,  state->xsize - x);             current_tile_length = min((INT32)tile_length, state->ysize - y);             for (tile_y = 0; tile_y < current_tile_length; tile_y++) {                 shuffler(                     (UINT8 *)im->image[tile_y + y] + x * im->pixelsize,                     state->buffer + tile_y * row_byte_size,   // <-- OOB stride                     current_tile_width                 );             }         }     } } ```  ```c // src/libImaging/Unpack.c:1288-1291 — copy4 (the crash site) static void copy4(UINT8 *out, const UINT8 *in, int pixels) {     /* RGBA, CMYK quadruples */     memcpy(out, in, 4 * pixels);   // <-- ASAN-detected READ here } ```  The PoC's tile metadata yields `tile_width = tile_length = 256`, `row_byte_size = 1024` (4 bytes/pixel × 256 pixels), and `tile_bytes_size = 196608` (which is 256·256·3 = three-channel-byte storage). The realloc'd buffer is 196608 bytes. The unpacker iterates `tile_y` from 0 to 255 and for the highest rows the source pointer `state->buffer + tile_y * 1024` already lies at or past offset 196608 — the very last row's `memcpy(in=buffer+255·1024, 1024)` reads 1024 bytes starting `260096 - 196608 = 63488` bytes past the allocation; ASAN flags the very first byte past the heap region (`READ of size 1024 at … 0 bytes after 196608-byte region`).  The mismatch is real: libtiff's `TIFFTileSize` returns the *packed* per-tile storage (which depends on the file's photometric/separation layout — it can legitimately be smaller than `row_byte_size × tile_length`), while the inner loop strides as if the buffer always equals `row_byte_size × tile_length`.   ## Attribution  This issue was found by Anthropic from using Claude to study security of open source projects, and I am from Ada Logics helping validate the found issues and report to maintainers. The data in this report has been reviewed manually.

``` ============================================================================ OOB read in TiffDecode.c tile and RGBA paths leaks heap memory into pixels Location: src/libImaging/TiffDecode.c:483  in _decodeTile() Commit:   a707c6b21c313880d0771e54965d142dd42358b6 ============================================================================ ```  Pillow reads past the end of a heap buffer when decoding certain malformed compressed TIFF files, and copies the bytes it reads into the pixels of the image it returns. An attacker who can get an application to open and load an image file, for example by uploading it to a service that returns thumbnails, previews or converted images, gets back fragments of that process's heap memory, including pointer values. A slightly larger file instead crashes the process. No special settings are needed, and nothing is written out of bounds.  The bug is in `_decodeTile()` and `_decodeAsRGBA()` in `src/libImaging/TiffDecode.c`. Both size their decode buffer from libtiff's view of the pixel layout (`TIFFTileSize()`/`TIFFTileRowSize()`, or `img.width * 4`). They then unpack each row with the unpacker that `TiffImagePlugin._setup()` chose from Pillow's own parse of the directory, and neither checks that the unpacker's input row fits inside the row libtiff produced. `_decodeStrip()` has exactly this check, added for OSS-Fuzz `crash-0da0` in 8.2.0, but the tile and RGBA paths never got it.  The two parsers can be made to disagree with a duplicated `PhotometricInterpretation` or `BitsPerSample` tag, because libtiff keeps the first occurrence and Pillow keeps the last. Pillow then unpacks 4 to 8 bytes per pixel from rows that libtiff filled with 1 to 4 bytes, so the last rows of each tile are read from beyond the buffer. The disclosed memory is a few tile rows past the buffer, and the attacker chooses the tile width. The amount does not grow with the number of tiles, because the buffer is reused for every tile.  The tile half was introduced in 1c295bf43 (first released in 8.2.0). The RGBA half was introduced in eb8c1206d, the CVE-2020-35654 fix (8.1.0).  The attached reproducer runs against an unmodified build. It writes three roughly 400-byte files that load without error, yet the last pixel rows of each change with glibc's malloc fill pattern and contain heap pointer bytes. A fourth file with a 65536x16 tile segfaults in `copy4` ← `_decodeTile` (`TiffDecode.c:483`) in most runs, depending on what is mapped after the buffer.  ## Details  `_decodeTile()` and `_decodeAsRGBA()` in `src/libImaging/TiffDecode.c` size `state->buffer` from what libtiff says it will produce (`TIFFTileSize()`, resp. `img.width * 4`), but unpack each row with the shuffler that `TiffImagePlugin._setup()` selected from Pillow's *own* parse of the IFD. Nothing in either function checks that the unpacker's input row (`width * state->bits / 8` bytes) fits inside the row libtiff wrote. `_decodeStrip()` has exactly that check; the other two do not. Whenever the two IFD parsers disagree about the pixel layout — a tag with the wrong count or type that libtiff ignores but Pillow accepts, or a duplicated `PhotometricInterpretation`/`BitsPerSample`/`SamplesPerPixel` entry (libtiff keeps the first occurrence, `ImageFileDirectory_v2.load()` the last) — the unpacker reads past the end of the heap buffer and the bytes it reads become pixels of the returned image. Any Pillow rawmode wider than libtiff's actual sample layout works (`RGBX`, `RGB;16N`, `RGBA;16N`, `I;32`, `F;32F`, …); `RGBA;16N` (64 bits/pixel) against 1-bit libtiff data is the largest ratio, where every row after the first of each tile is read almost entirely from beyond the buffer. Rows 13–15 of the result contain bytes that lie 16, 32 and 48 bytes past the 256-byte tile buffer: decoding the same file twice under `MALLOC_PERTURB_=85` and `=170` yields identical rows 0–12 and different bytes in rows 13–15 (`aa` vs `55`, i.e. glibc's fill pattern). The over-read bytes are copied into the image's pixel rows, so a service that returns a thumbnail, preview or converted image hands adjacent heap memory back to the uploader, heap pointer values included — up to three libtiff tile rows past the buffer for the `RGBX`-over-8-bit case, with the tile row length (`TileWidth`) chosen by the attacker. `state->buffer` is allocated once and reused for every tile, so each tile re-reads the same region past that one buffer; the distinct heap disclosed per image is about `(unpacker_bpp / libtiff_bpp − 1)` tile rows and does not grow with the tile count. With a wide tile the read runs off the mapping and the process segfaults instead (the 65536x16 case crashes the stock build in most runs, depending on what is mapped after the buffer), taking down the whole worker rather than one request. Writes go to the correctly sized `Imaging` rows, so this is disclosure / crash, not memory corruption.  This is the same family as CVE-2020-35654 (Pillow and libtiff interpreting a YCbCr IFD differently in `TiffDecode.c`); that fix and the later `crash-0da0` fix closed the write and the strip-path read, but the tile path and the RGBA path still trust Pillow's rawmode over libtiff's row size. The tile-path gap was introduced in 1c295bf43c3a ("Check for dimensions and sizes to fit into int", 2021-01-25), which switched `_decodeTile()` from a buffer sized by Pillow's unpacker to `TIFFTileSize()`/`TIFFTileRowSize()`; it is first in Pillow 8.2.0. The `_decodeAsRGBA()` half dates from eb8c1206d6b1 ("Fix CVE-2020-35654 - OOB Write in TiffDecode.c"), first in 8.1.0.  ## Reproducing  Run `repro` (a single Python 3 script) against the installed, unmodified Pillow. No sanitizer build is needed. It writes four TIFFs into a temporary directory, decodes each one in a child process, and removes the directory at the end.  The script writes its TIFFs byte by byte with a small classic-TIFF writer. Each file has a single IFD and a single Deflate-compressed block. Deflate is only there so the file is decoded by libtiff and `TiffDecode.c`. Every pixel byte in the compressed data is defined, so the decoded image should not depend on anything else in the process:  - **`tile_count2.tif`**: a 16x16, 1-sample, 8-bit tile with `PhotometricInterpretation` written as SHORT count 2, `(6, 6)`. This variant also applies to released versions. - **`ycbcr_dup.tif`**: the 16x16 strip with `BitsPerSample` `8,8,8` then `16,16,16` and `PhotometricInterpretation` `6` then `2`. libtiff decodes 8-bit YCbCr through `_decodeAsRGBA()` (4 bytes per pixel), and Pillow unpacks `RGB;16N` with `unpackRGB16L` (6 bytes per pixel). - **`tile_big.tif`**: the `tile_count2.tif` layout with a single 65536x16 tile. If the two outputs differ, bytes from beyond the decode buffer have become pixels. In that case it prints the first differing offset and the bytes around it from both runs. On this tree all three differ in their last rows: the `aa`/`55` fill bytes show up, along with heap pointer bytes. The script then decodes `tile_big.tif` and checks for a SIGSEGV (exit status -11). Otherwise it is `OK`.  ## Suggested fix  The attached patch restores the `_decodeStrip()` invariant (the unpacker's input row must fit inside libtiff's row) in the two sibling decoders in `src/libImaging/TiffDecode.c`, at the point where each one sizes its buffer:  - `_decodeTile()` computes `unpacker_row_byte_size = ((tsize_t)tile_width * state->bits / planes + 7) / 8` (the `tsize_t` cast keeps the product out of 32-bit arithmetic, so the `TILEWIDTH = 2^26+16` case above cannot wrap past the check on 64-bit builds). It reuses that value for the existing `TIFFTileSize()` sanity check, as `_decodeStrip()` does for strips. After that check and before the `realloc`, it fails with `IMAGING_CODEC_BROKEN` when `unpacker_row_byte_size > row_byte_size` (`TIFFTileRowSize()`). - `_decodeAsRGBA()` fails with `IMAGING_CODEC_BROKEN` when `state->bits > 32`, because `TIFFRGBAImage` rows are always 32 bits per pixel. This check runs before `TIFFRGBAImageBegin()` and any allocation.  With the patch, the tile and RGBA files fail `load()` with `OSError: decoder error -2`, the same result the equivalent strip file already gets. The patch also adds a regression test to `Tests/test_file_libtiff.py` (`test_unpacker_row_wider_than_libtiff_row`). The test embeds the count-2 tile and the duplicated-tag YCbCr strip as base64, following the file's existing convention. It never calls `Image._decompression_bomb_check()` on the scaled size. The only check is the one `Image.open()` ran on the unscaled size, so a file declaring 9000×9000 passes, and `load(scale=2)` then asks Ghostscript for 18000×18000 (3.6× `MAX_IMAGE_PIXELS`). A file declaring 18000×18000 directly would be refused before Ghostscript ever ran. `DecompressionBombError` fires only when Pillow reopens the output file, so Pillow's own in-process allocation stays bounded and there is no memory corruption.
